findings.population: healthy adults and patients with sexual dysfunction (4 RCTs)
findings.finding_summary: This systematic review found four eligible RCTs: two suggested positive effects on sexual desire or dysfunction (healthy menopausal women; healthy adult men) and one showed benefit in erectile dysfunction, while one trial in healthy cyclists found no effect; the authors conclude the evidence is limited.
findings.limitations: the authors state the number of trials, total sample size, and methodological quality are too limited to draw firm conclusions

findings.population: men in clinical trials of Tribulus terrestris supplementation
findings.finding_summary: This systematic review of clinical trials found no robust evidence that Tribulus terrestris increases testosterone levels in men, with only low-level evidence for improving erectile function.
findings.limitations: a strong honest null for the most common marketing claim; isolated positive signals exist in other populations (e.g., premenopausal women) with very low certainty

findings.population: men in randomized clinical trials of fenugreek extract (4 trials)
findings.finding_summary: This meta-analysis of four randomized clinical trials found fenugreek extract supplementation had a significant effect on total serum testosterone in men.
findings.limitations: only four trials, largely of proprietary extracts; magnitude and clinical meaning of the change remain modest

findings.population: women with PMS or PMDD in randomized trials
findings.finding_summary: This systematic review found seven of eight PMS trials reported Vitex agnus-castus superior to placebo (and to pyridoxine and magnesium oxide comparators); in PMDD, one trial found Vitex equivalent to fluoxetine while another favored fluoxetine.
findings.limitations: the wider meta-analytic literature flags high risk of bias, high heterogeneity, and possible publication bias — the large pooled effect should be read cautiously

findings.population: menopausal women (16 studies, 2,027 women; ~40 mg/day for ~23 weeks)
findings.finding_summary: This Cochrane review (16 studies, 2,027 women, average 40 mg/day for 23 weeks) concluded there is insufficient evidence to support black cohosh for menopausal symptoms, while judging further research justified.
findings.limitations: insufficient-evidence verdict rather than proof of no effect; preparation heterogeneity is substantial

findings.endpoint: total and free testosterone in resistance-trained men
findings.population: resistance-trained men (n=24, randomized to placebo, 3 g/day, or 6 g/day)
findings.finding_summary: In this randomized controlled trial, 6 g/day D-aspartic acid significantly REDUCED total and free testosterone in resistance-trained men, while 3 g/day had no effect — the opposite of the marketing claim built on earlier untrained-population data.
findings.limitations: short trial; the longer 12-week trial in the same population also found no testosterone or training benefit at 6 g/day

findings.endpoint: menopausal hot flash frequency and severity
findings.population: perimenopausal and postmenopausal women in double-blind RCTs
findings.finding_summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis found extracted or synthesized soy isoflavone supplements reduced hot flash frequency by 20.6% and severity by 26.2% versus placebo, with supplements providing more than 18.8 mg genistein over twice as potent as lower-genistein products.
findings.limitations: effect size is meaningful but smaller than hormone therapy; genistein content — rarely labeled — moderates the effect
